chapter: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
title: Benny Morton's seriousness, Jimmy Harrison's shake and his memory
summary: Morton counted rests rather than talk, learned Harrison's tone shake, enjoyed Hawkins' tricks and has an uncanny memory and reading ability.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: I have -- he was in Fletcher's band. He was in Don Redman's band, and I had the pleasure of being with him all of on these occasions, and he could always play. But he was very serious about his playing, you know, and he's another one, naturally, by playing, he couldn't talk and play, even though -- if he had four or five bars out, he's counting. And he

He wouldn't know knew what you were talking about because I checked with him on it. So -- but he did -- Benny played these fine chords, and he was in Fletcher's band when Jimmy Harrison, the great trombonist, was there, and he learned a lot of things from Jimmy because he was just a youngster. And Jimmy played, man, there, and Jimmy had a little -- Jimmy Harrison had a little nanny, little shake, as we called it, in his tone, just enough to be pleasing to the ear, and Benny loved this, and he always wanted to get this little shake, you know?
And he did, because I know when he came over to Don Redman, he had that.

Of course, he really was a great things player, and he was a nice guy -- always talked to you. He was an interesting guy to talk to, and, of course, we talked music and all those things. And he had a great sense of humor, and he -- because in the band, talked to, you know, and he would get a kick -- he would go on, and those guys would just fall out when Hawk would play tricks on the guys, you know, and Jimmy, you know --
-- and he would participate in them, but he'd throw his hands up and shake his head, you know, and

all this and that, drop his head. But he is one of the few guys that I think is living that, if you take him right along here with me, he would know all these things I'm telling you now because his memory was uncanny too. I say too -- I cut off the too. His memory was uncanny.
Listen, yours is too, man. It's knocking me out.

But Benny Morton has always been a great reader. I'm telling you these things about it because him [set music up] before. I've seen (inaudible) of his work. No sweat. I think he played the Metropole too. Any time, you know, the Metropole was a great place for guys where a lot of -- whoever owned that (inaudible). If they were good friends of the musicians, If they didn't have any jobs, they always could go to the Metropole and play, and they'd play down there, and jam jazz and all that stuff. So Benny played there too. So I hope I see him this summer because I plan to take a little trip to New York, and he's one of the many that I'm going to look up --
You've got a lot, of them.
